tip.title: Wake at the same time on weekends
tip.why: Sleeping in on Saturday feels like catching up, but your body clock reads it as a flight east and back every week. Till Roenneberg's group coined the term social jetlag for this gap between weekday and weekend sleep timing; in a 2012 Current Biology analysis of sleep logs from more than 65,000 Europeans, each hour of social jetlag went with a higher chance of being overweight, independent of how long people slept. Later work has tied the same gap to worse mood and Monday grogginess, which is just the clock catching up.
how: Keep your weekend alarm within an hour of your weekday one, even after a late night; make up lost sleep with an early bedtime or a short afternoon nap instead.
Get outside within an hour of waking: morning light is what anchors the clock, and a cloudy day still counts.
If Friday night runs late, protect the wake time and accept one short night; the clock cares more about when you get up than how long you slept.
tip.ask: How far did this morning drift from your weekday alarm, and what would you do with that hour if it had not?

markets.headline: Stocks slipped Friday but still booked their first winning week since October: the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,561.67 as hot producer prices pushed the 10-year yield to 5.15%, Nvidia closed below $4 trillion, Tesla gave back 1.8% and SpaceX dipped into a Starship flight that reached orbit but lost its booster.
points: The S&P 500 fell 30.73 points (0.40%) to 7,561.67, the Nasdaq dropped 0.91% to 25,136.27 and the Dow added 0.10% to 52,347.55, the only major index up on the day. For the week the S&P 500 gained about 2.5% and the Nasdaq 2.3%, the best week since August, and breadth was positive with 314 S&P members higher.

October producer prices rose 0.3% on the month against a 0.4% forecast, but the 6.5% annual rate is the highest since November 2022, and Treasuries sold off again: the 10-year yield closed near 5.15% after touching 5.17%, its highest since October, with the weekly rise of roughly 26 to 30 basis points the biggest since April 2025. A December hike is fully priced and a January move largely so; the dollar index hit its highest since April 2025 and WTI settled at $88.56, down 2.5% on the week.

Nvidia fell 2.01% to 162.85 after HSBC cut it to Hold on CEO uncertainty, taking its market value under $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 and its weekly loss to about 12.8%, a sixth straight losing week. AMD gave back 8.75% of Thursday's pop, and semicap names KLA and Lam lost 5 to 6% after Applied Materials' beat-and-raise quarter drew a round of target cuts.

Tesla fell 7.23 (1.82%) to 390.22, still up about 8.9% on the week, as investors weighed Bloomberg's report that a SpaceX merger could be announced as soon as December but would need a majority of all outstanding shares, a hurdle Musk himself called high. Intel lost 1.54 (2.52%) to 59.66 on about 102 million shares as analysts asked what Huang's exit means for Nvidia's roughly $13 billion Intel stake. SpaceX slipped 0.83 (0.59%) to 139.11 before Starship Flight 15 lifted off at 2:47 PM PT; Ship 42 reached orbit and released all 26 Starlink V3 satellites, but Booster 22 aborted its tower catch over a guidance problem and burned in the Gulf, and the shares traded down about 2% after hours.

pick.name: Applied Materials
pick.theme: The biggest US chip-equipment maker just posted a record quarter and guided above the Street, and the stock sold off anyway
pick.what: Applied Materials is the largest US semiconductor-equipment company: it sells the deposition, etch, implant, inspection and advanced-packaging tools that TSMC, Samsung, Intel and Micron use to make leading-edge logic, DRAM and high-bandwidth memory. A services arm of roughly $2 billion a quarter maintains and upgrades the installed base, which smooths out the equipment cycle.
pick.why: After the November 12 close the company reported record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $10.41 billion, up 53% from a year earlier and ahead of the $10.30 billion consensus, with record adjusted earnings of $4.16 a share against $4.06 expected; full-year revenue was $34.45 billion, up 21%. It guided the January quarter to $11.1 billion plus or minus $500 million and $4.35 a share, both above consensus, and said semiconductor systems should grow more than 40% in calendar 2026 with another record in 2027. The stock still fell 2.74% to 370.50 on Friday as JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and Needham trimmed targets while keeping Buy ratings; TipRanks shows a Strong Buy consensus with 24 of 25 analysts at Buy and an average target of $649.30, StockAnalysis also has Strong Buy with a $620.78 average, and the shares sit about 50% below the 52-week high of 739.67. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: The stock has lost half its value since June and about 28% in a month, and the whole equipment group is de-rating as targets fall even with Buy ratings intact (KLA and Lam fell 5 to 6% on Friday). A 10-year yield at 5.15% and a fully priced December hike weigh on long-duration growth names, Nvidia's leadership turmoil hangs over the AI-capex complex, the low end of the new guide sits below consensus, management flagged capacity pinch points and China export exposure, and the January quarter is a 14-week period that flatters the comparison. Sources also disagreed on Friday's close (Yahoo showed 359.38), so check the print.

btc.summary: Cowen's newest video, posted Friday and titled Bitcoin Drops Below $70k, treats the break as the four-year cycle doing what it does rather than a surprise, and he expects the weakness to run for a few more weeks at least, into the December Fed meeting. The question he cares about now is whether the eventual low lands above or below the realized price, the average cost basis of all coins, which sits in the mid-$50,000s: a deeper low that undercuts it would reset the on-chain indicators and set up a proper bull market in 2027, while a higher low would probably only hold prices up for three to six months before another retest. He also points at the Anthropic IPO as one reason the slide accelerated, arguing that investors pull cash out of risk assets ahead of big offerings, and his practical stance is unchanged: dollar-cost average instead of trying to call the exact bottom.

articles.title: Starship made orbit and lost its booster; the ship catch is today
body: Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase at 2:47 PM Pacific on Friday, and the mission split in two. Ship 42 reached orbit, only the second time a Starship has done so, and about 40 minutes in it pushed all **26 Starlink V3 satellites** out through the payload door at roughly 275 km. Booster 22 never came back to the tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff the booster called off its own catch. SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said on the webcast that it "aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected", GNC being guidance, navigation and control, and it diverted to a pre-planned splashdown zone in the Gulf, where Spaceflight Now watched it blow up on contact. SpaceX has not published a cause; one informal account blames an engine-out during the boostback burn, and that is unconfirmed.
The FAA said SpaceX's decisions were within approved flight criteria, and no mishap investigation had been announced by Saturday morning, so the program is not grounded.

The bigger prize is still in play. After a 22-hour coast, Ship 42 is scheduled to come home to the Starbase tower at about **1:20 PM Pacific today**, the first attempt ever to catch a Starship upper stage, with a Pacific splashdown as the fallback if a final go/no-go check fails. CNN's live blog quoted SpaceX's heat-shield team saying the shield is in a good posture based on ground tracking and satellite imagery, and Musk put a successful catch at more likely than not.

SpaceX stock, which trades as SPCX, closed Friday at **$139.11**, down 0.6%, with the launch itself after the bell; it slipped about 2% more after hours once the booster abort was clear. Morgan Stanley had called Flight 15 one of the most significant catalysts in the company's history, and the shares sit roughly 38% below their peak.

For the orbital-compute watchers: SemiAnalysis reported, via Data Center Dynamics, that SpaceX is designing a custom Nvidia Vera Rubin rack it calls Kessel for both ground and orbital use, the first hardware-level detail on its space data center plans.

If the ship comes down on the chopsticks this afternoon, SpaceX will have recovered an orbital-class vehicle and its heat shield intact for the first time, the step Musk has called the hardest remaining problem. If it misses, the fallback is open water and a long look at the tiles. No date for Flight 16 has been announced.

articles.title: OpenAI folds its robotics team into the model groups
body: OpenAI has dissolved its standalone robotics team, Fortune reported Friday. Robotics research now reports to chief research officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware staff move into the Applied organization run by president Greg Brockman. The company told Fortune its general models, including the one it calls GPT-6 Astra, had shown they could handle robotics directly, and said it is not leaving the field: a first public humanoid demo is still **targeted for 2027**.

It is the second time OpenAI has shut a dedicated robotics group: the first ended in 2020 for lack of robot data, the group was rebuilt in 2024, and the Figure partnership ended in February 2025. The bet now is that a frontier model absorbs embodied AI as one more capability rather than a separate stack.

A rare public endurance test in Shanghai showed how far the field still has to go. The Robot Report wrote this week that AgiBot ran six G2 wheeled humanoids for 24 straight hours in a working convenience store, from Nov 2 to Nov 3, livestreamed to more than two million viewers. The robots completed **1,730 tasks** and four of six passed the company's own assessment; the cleaning robot wandered off after meeting an overflowing bin, left the store and did not come back.

New entrants keep arriving. Genki Robotics, the Tokyo startup founded by Android creator Andy Rubin, showed its humanoid for the first time at a meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Humanoids Daily reported; the company said the unit was assembled over the weekend and walked for the first time on Monday, with a first product model aimed at year-end.

On the research side, Apple published results for a controller called HALO that hit 91% success across 360 single-task trials on a stock Unitree G1 in unfamiliar rooms, per humanoid.guide: a paper, not a product.

The money is less cheerful. Agility Robotics, the first pure-play humanoid stock, fell again Friday to about **$7**, roughly 40% below its Nov 5 debut close, after J.P. Morgan started coverage at Neutral with an $11 target. And the Financial Times reported that Foundation Robotics, the Eric Trump-backed startup, is in talks with Israel's military about up to 1,000 of its Phantom MK-1 humanoids for patrolling tunnels in Gaza; Israel has not chosen the robots and nothing says they would be armed.

Taken together: the frontier labs think the model is the robot, the field tests say the robot still gets lost, and the public market is pricing the gap. Figure, Tesla Optimus and Meta's prototype had no new developments this week.

articles.title: Nvidia sounds out Arm's chief as Anthropic shuts China out of its IPO
body: Nvidia's board has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a possible successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported Friday; Haas ran Nvidia's computing products group for seven years before joining Arm. The board told Reuters it is still choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged anyone. Inside the company, more than **1,600 employees** commented on an internal post urging Huang's reinstatement.

The stock had its first full day of trading on the news. HSBC cut Nvidia to Hold with a $170 target, saying the shares will struggle until a permanent CEO is named; Nvidia closed at $162.85, down 2%, under $4 trillion in market value for the first time since July 2025. Monday's third-quarter report, Colette Kress's first as interim chief, is now the event of the week.

Anthropic's listing kept gathering detail. Bloomberg reported that institutional investors based in mainland China and Hong Kong have been told they cannot place orders, and that bankers are steering allocations toward existing backers. At the top of the **$70 to $78** range, the offering plus the private placement would raise $90.4 billion; pricing is set for Nov 18 and a Nasdaq debut as ANT on Nov 19, with the book roughly six times covered.

OpenAI, meanwhile, launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents buy things on a user's behalf, starting with US Pro subscribers over 18 and working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa; the company says the agents never see card details and it is not taking a cut for now.

Two model releases from Wednesday deserve a mention. Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, the everyday successor to Gemini 3.8 Flash beneath the larger Carbon model, claiming 2.5 times faster task completion at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 for output. Thinking Machines Lab posted the weights of Inkling 2 Small on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0: a **594-billion-parameter** mixture-of-experts model with 17 billion active, image input and a million-token context that needs about 500 GB of GPU memory to run.

What it means: Nvidia's succession is now a market variable with a date attached, Anthropic's offering is being run as a geopolitical allocation as much as a sale, and the model cadence has not slowed for either.

articles.title: Tesla pulls the $41,990 Model Y as merger talk cools a five-day run
body: Tesla removed the $41,990 Model Y all-wheel-drive trim from its US configurator this week without an announcement, Electrek and TeslaNorth reported. The cheapest configurable all-wheel-drive car is now the Premium at $49,990, an **$8,000** jump, while the $39,990 rear-drive model remains; the trim lasted about nine months after its February debut, and some inventory units are still listed.

The Cybertruck lineup shrank to one. Electrek reported the Cyberbeast is now **$109,990**, 57% above the entry price in August, with the Dual Motor and Premium trims gone from the configurator; Tesla has not said whether queued orders for those trims will be built. That follows this week's reversal on production, which now runs through the end of summer 2027.

On the SpaceX combination, day two added no terms. Musk said both companies have formed independent special committees and that he is staying out of the talks because he owns shares in both, adding that calling a merger a certainty "would be overstating it." Benzinga noted the Dec 3 annual meeting has no merger vote and that Polymarket bettors doubt a December deal, while Motley Fool's math says buying Tesla at market with no premium would take about 11.2 billion new SpaceX shares. Texas's incoming attorney general promised tremendous scrutiny.
Tesla shares fell 1.8% to **$390.22**, ending a five-day winning streak but still up about 9% on the week, with the merger uncertainty and the broader chip selloff both cited.

The robotaxi fleet keeps growing: 573 Cybercabs were registered in Tesla's Texas fleet as of Nov 9, up from 463 earlier this month, across eight cities including Fort Worth and San Antonio. A single retailer blog described Cybercab orders opening to select customers at $29,990 with a $299 monthly autonomy subscription inside robotaxi geofences; that is unconfirmed. Unsupervised FSD for customer cars remains tied to version 15 around the second quarter of 2027.
What it means: trims are disappearing as Tesla steers production toward higher-margin slots, and the merger is a December question with no filing behind it yet. Optimus had no news this week.

articles.title: Microsoft's day-long outage; chip earnings that beat and still fell
body: Microsoft's work suite went down for close to a full day. Starting around 8 AM Pacific on Thursday, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and SharePoint failed for users in **74 countries** within the first hour, per Downdetector; some offices fell back to fax and at least one European bond repurchase was halted. Microsoft blamed server issues, ruled out an attack and ruled out AI as a cause, paused all deployments and restarted servers; by late Friday it said email was approaching normal, nearly 24 hours later. The stock closed up 0.17%.

Two chip-adjacent companies beat and were punished anyway. Applied Materials posted record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $10.41 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.16 a share, both ahead of estimates, and guided the next quarter to about $11.1 billion, yet the shares fell 2.7% on Friday as a string of banks trimmed targets while keeping Buy ratings. Cisco beat on every headline number but product orders grew 21% against 35% the prior quarter, the chief executive called AI orders lumpy, and the stock fell despite a higher $9 billion target for hyperscaler AI revenue.

The macro backdrop was the hot producer price report: October wholesale prices rose 0.3% on the month, a touch below forecast, but **6.5%** from a year earlier, the largest annual increase since November 2022. The 10-year Treasury yield closed near 5.15% after touching 5.17%, futures put a Fed hike on Dec 9 at a certainty with a second priced for January, and the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to 7,561.67 while the Nasdaq lost 0.9%. The week still ended higher, the first winning week since October.

Elsewhere, Cerebras surprised with a profit on $231 million of revenue, Nebius extended its post-earnings slide with a 12% drop, and Apple touched an intraday record of $360.80. The FT reported Amazon has revived its deal for 600 megawatts at Fermi America's Texas campus, so far only a non-binding letter of intent.
What it means: the outage is a reminder of how much of the working world runs on one vendor, and the earnings pattern says the AI trade now needs beats and clean guidance just to stay flat.

articles.title: Bitcoin near $67,000 into the weekend as ETF outflows hit day seven
body: Bitcoin found no bounce after Friday's break below $70,000. It traded between about **$67,000 and $67,400** early Saturday, under its 200-week moving average for the first time in years, down more than 10% on the week and roughly 46% below the October 2025 record of $126,080. About $1.26 billion of leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours, most of them longs.

The ETF bleed is now a streak. US spot bitcoin funds lost **$185.4 million** on Thursday, a seventh straight day of outflows per Farside, with IBIT accounting for $143.5 million and FBTC for $41.9 million and every other fund flat; IBIT's own streak is eleven days. The week came to roughly $1.07 billion out and November to more than $2 billion, against about $55 billion of net inflows since the funds launched. Ether funds took in a token $2.4 million.

The driver is the same one hitting tech: a 6.5% annual producer-price print, a 10-year yield at 5.15% and a December Fed hike that futures now treat as certain. Benjamin Cowen, in a Friday video, added another: investors tend to raise cash ahead of a giant IPO, and Anthropic prices on Nov 18.

Strategy's index exit is now dated. MSCI will delete the company from its USA, World and ACWI indexes at the close on **Nov 30**, and Strategy estimates index funds will have to sell about 13 million shares. The company holds roughly 848,500 bitcoin at an average cost of $75,456, so the stash is under water for the first time in years; commentators argue the real risk is slower buying rather than forced selling, and no new purchase was disclosed this week.

On regulation, Forbes concluded the CLARITY Act, the crypto market-structure bill that failed a 49 to 50 cloture vote in September, is effectively tabled until January after the Democratic midterm sweep.
What comes next: traders are watching whether $66,000 holds, with the Anthropic pricing on Tuesday and the Fed on Dec 9 as the two dated events. Cowen's own read is on the Bitcoin page.

articles.title: Blood NAD doesn't fall with age, a large study finds
body: The premise behind a billion-dollar supplement category took a hit on Friday. A Nature Metabolism study of **1,068 adults**, reported by Medical Xpress, found that blood levels of NAD, the coenzyme that NMN and NR pills are meant to restore, do not decline with age in healthy people. They were lower in people with cardiovascular disease, particularly hypertension, which points to NAD as a marker of heart health rather than of aging itself. The study did not test whether supplements help anyone.

A Monash University team writing in Immunity identified granzyme K, a protein released by immune cells, as a driver of age-related damage in the heart, liver and kidneys. Mice engineered without it showed **less organ aging** even though their immune systems aged normally, which separates the damage from the aging of the immune system that produces it. It is mouse data, and the human role is unproven.

In Aging Cell, a Chinese group showed that the enzyme USP25 strips ubiquitin tags from SIRT1, the longevity-linked deacetylase, which lowers its activity and lets p53 and PGC1-alpha accumulate acetyl marks that push cells into senescence. Mice lacking USP25 had fewer age-related changes, and a cell-penetrating peptide the authors call pSirt1-4, which blocks the USP25 and SIRT1 interaction, reduced senescence in cell models. Fight Aging flagged it as a plausible drug target.

Also circulating this week, though the paper is from July: Dudley Lamming's review of more than 350 studies on protein and amino-acid restriction, which finds that lower protein extends lifespan in flies and rodents without cutting calories, with short human trials showing fat loss and better fasting glucose. The human lifespan effect remains unproven.

What it means: two of the week's findings subtract from popular stories (NAD declines, immune aging as the whole story) and two add candidate targets. No trial readouts, FDA decisions or major funding rounds surfaced, and Loyal's dog drug still awaits its 2027 review.

vocab.def: Relating to or living on the banks of a river or stream; the strip of land, plants and animals that depend on a waterway.

cards.b: Latin ripa ('riverbank'), the same root as the Spanish ribera and the French rive
riverside, streamside, bankside, littoral (for a lake or sea)
the willows along Stevens Creek, a wildlife corridor, the law of who owns a riverbank

examples: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.
Water rights here are riparian: if your land touches the stream, you get a share of it.
vocab.ex: The riparian corridor along the creek was the only green line left on the map by August.

vocab.def: Glowing or flickering softly over a surface; of wit or light, playing lightly and brilliantly without heat.

cards.b: Latin lambere ('to lick'): a flame that licks across a surface without burning it
glowing, flickering, luminous, softly radiant
late sun on the bay, a gas flame on a stove, a friend's light and quick humor

examples: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.
Her lambent wit kept the review going for two hours without anyone noticing the time.
vocab.ex: By 4:30 the lambent light off the salt ponds made even the parking lot look painted.

vocab.def: Casually unconcerned; carefree in a way that shows a light, almost careless lack of worry.

cards.b: French insouciant, from in- ('not') and soucier ('to care'), from Latin sollicitare ('to disturb')
nonchalant, carefree, breezy, unbothered
a surfer shrugging at a wipeout, a founder joking through a bad quarter, a cat on a warm car hood

examples: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.
There's an insouciant charm to a city that closes its best street for a Sunday market.
vocab.ex: He gave an insouciant shrug when the demo robot fell over, and the room relaxed with him.

vocab.def: The tendency to see meaningful patterns or connections in random or unrelated data.

cards.b: Coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958, from Greek apo- ('away from') and phainein ('to show')
patternicity, false pattern, seeing faces in clouds
a backtest that only looks predictive, a 'trend' in three data points, a conspiracy theory

examples: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.
Robot logs invite apophenia: every glitch looks like a pattern until you count.
vocab.ex: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.

vocab.def: Calm self-confidence, especially in a tense or difficult situation.

cards.b: French 'à plomb', 'according to the plumb line', meaning upright and steady
poise, composure, assurance
handling pressure gracefully: a demo gone wrong, a hard question, a surprise

examples: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.
The robot demo failed, but he recovered with aplomb.
vocab.ex: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.

vocab.def: Impossible to avoid or escape; certain to happen no matter what you do.

cards.b: Latin 'ineluctabilis', from in- (not) + eluctari (to struggle out of)
inescapable, unavoidable, inevitable
fate, deadlines, or facts that no amount of effort changes

examples: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.
He felt the ineluctable pull of the old neighborhood.
vocab.ex: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.

vocab.def: A very fine, light, delicate material, like spider silk; or anything that feels that thin and airy.

cards.b: Middle English; often traced to 'goose summer', the warm autumn days when floating spider silk is seen
filmy, sheer, diaphanous
cobwebs in morning light, thin fabric, or something fragile and barely there

examples: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.
She wore a gossamer scarf that moved with every breath of wind.
vocab.ex: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.

spanish.meaning: What a drag / I really can't be bothered
spanish.note: Hueva is literally fish roe, but in Mexico it means laziness or boredom. '¡Qué hueva!' is the groan you let out when something tedious lands on you: a rainy Sunday errand, a long meeting, a form. Among friends only; it is mildly crude, so skip it with your boss or your partner's parents.

cards.en: I can't be bothered / it bores me

parts.en: it makes me not want to

dialog.es: ¿Vamos al súper? Ya no hay nada en el refri.
dialog.en: Shall we go to the store? There's nothing left in the fridge.

dialog.es: ¡Qué hueva! Está lloviendo y acabo de sentarme.
dialog.en: What a drag! It's raining and I just sat down.

dialog.es: Pues ni modo, o vamos o cenamos cereal.
dialog.en: Well, no choice: we go or we have cereal for dinner.

dialog.es: Va, me quito la hueva y nos vamos.
dialog.en: Fine, I'll shake it off and let's go.

spanish.use: Say it, with a groan, when a boring task shows up on a day you wanted off; swap in 'qué flojera' when you are not sure how casual the room is.

spanish.note: Cañón is literally 'cannon' or 'canyon', but in Mexico 'está cañón' means something is hard, heavy or impressive: a tough exam, a brutal commute, a wild story. Tone decides whether it's a complaint or admiration.

cards.en: Same idea, cruder; only with close friends

parts.en: a cannon shot; a hit song

dialog.en: How did the interview go?

dialog.es: Está cañón, me hicieron tres pruebas técnicas.
dialog.en: It's intense, they gave me three technical tests.
And did you pass?

dialog.es: Creo que sí, pero me dejaron hecho polvo.
dialog.en: I think so, but they wore me out.

spanish.use: Say it when someone describes a hard day, a steep trail or a big bill, or with a grin when a demo blows you away.

spanish.note: Literally 'what a bear', but in Mexico it's the everyday way to say 'how embarrassing' or 'how awkward', about yourself or someone else. 'Hacer el oso' is to embarrass yourself in public.

cards.en: I'm embarrassed / it makes me shy

parts.en: to make a fool of yourself

dialog.es: Le dije 'mamá' a la maestra enfrente de todos.
dialog.en: I called the teacher 'mom' in front of everyone.
How embarrassing! And what did you do?

dialog.es: Nada, me puse rojo y me senté.
dialog.en: Nothing, I turned red and sat down.

dialog.es: Ya ni modo, mañana nadie se acuerda.
dialog.en: Oh well, tomorrow nobody will remember.

spanish.use: Say it with a wince when someone trips, waves at the wrong person or replies-all by mistake.

spanish.note: Literally 'to little', but in Mexico it's the everyday way to say 'really?' or 'you're kidding' when something surprises you. Flip it to '¿a poco no?' and it means 'right?' or 'isn't it?'

cards.en: No way! / Don't make it up!

dialog.en: They offered me a job in Guadalajara.
Really? That's great!
Yes, I start in January.
Well, congratulations, we have to celebrate.

spanish.use: Say it with raised eyebrows the moment someone surprises you.

spanish.note: Literally 'it's of hairs', but in Mexican slang 'de pelos' means excellent or really good. Use it for food, plans, music, anything you like.

dialog.en: Did you try the new tacos?
Yes, they're awesome!
Shall we go again tomorrow?
Deal, we'll go tomorrow.

spanish.use: Say it when something is better than you expected.

spanish.meaning: I can't be bothered to go out
spanish.note: 'Flojera' is laziness, but in Mexican Spanish 'me da flojera' is a relaxed way to say you don't feel like doing something. It isn't a harsh judgment of yourself. Swap in any verb: 'me da flojera cocinar'.

dialog.en: Shall we go to the movies tonight?
Ugh, I can't be bothered to go out.

dialog.es: Pedimos pizza y vemos algo en casa.
dialog.en: We'll order pizza and watch something at home.
Now that's a great idea!

spanish.use: Say it when a plan sounds fine but your couch sounds better.

options: I can't be bothered to go out

spanish.meaning: I like your friend (he's easy to get along with)
spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish 'caer bien' means that someone strikes you as likeable. It's about the person's vibe, not romance. The opposite is 'caer mal' or, more bluntly, 'caer gordo'.

dialog.en: What did you think of Luis?

dialog.es: Me cae bien tu amigo, es muy relajado.
dialog.en: I like your friend, he's very laid back.
Yeah, he always makes me laugh.

dialog.es: Invítalo otra vez, me cae bien.
dialog.en: Invite him again, I like him.

spanish.use: Say it after meeting someone you got along with, to tell a friend your first impression.

dare.title: Go hear the creek running
dare.why: Yesterday's storm is the first real water Stevens Creek has had since spring, and today is your only dry window: the showers quit this morning and the next storm lands Sunday morning. Walk or bike to the Stevens Creek Trail where it crosses the creek, anywhere between Dale Avenue and Shoreline, lean on the rail and stand there for ten full minutes with the phone in your pocket. Sunset is 4:58, so the hour before that is the one with light on the water.

place.name: Stevens Creek Trail
place.sub: Mountain View, about 10 minutes by bike from downtown

dare.worth: A creek that is a dry ditch nine months of the year turns into a loud brown river for about two days after the first storm, and almost nobody goes to look. Standing still by moving water is the cheapest reset there is; the Kaplans called it soft fascination, attention that rests you instead of draining you.
dare.src: Rachel and Stephen Kaplan · attention restoration theory

swap.title: Leave a book in a Little Free Library

swap.worth: Somebody you will never meet gets a book with a stranger's note in it, which is a better way to be remembered than most things you will do this week.
